questions.stem: A 34-year-old man developed pustular, suppurative, nodular lesions over his arms that increased in size and quantity over 3 months. He had severe myasthenia gravis and had been taking prednisone 40 mg per day for 18 months. The lesions were unresponsive to a 14-day course of doxycycline and a subsequent 14-day course of oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. On examination:
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ascending lymphangitis secondary to Nocardia spp. infection

questions.explanation: Nodular granulomatous perifolliculitis (Majocchi’s granuloma) Nodular granulomatous perifolliculitis (Majocchi’s granuloma) occurs when dermatophytes invade hair follicles leading to granulomas and/or suppuration. The same organisms which are responsible for tinea corporis and/or pedis (Trichophyton rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, Epidermophyton floccosum, etc.) are involved. Occlusion, trauma to skin (e.g., shaving), use of topical steroids on unsuspected tinea, and immunocompromised states increase risk. It presents as subacute to chronic nodular lesions that progressively increase in size and number after dermatophyte invasion of hair follicles. Look for cluster(s) of pustules/ papules/nodules within erythematous scaling plaques, that may resemble bacterial furuncles or carbuncles. Treatment requires systemic antifungals.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q49

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of fever and productive cough. He had a deceased donor renal transplant 7 months ago. He was taking tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone. On exam his temperature was 38.6°C Investigations: CXR: left lower lobe nodule with central cavitation Sputum microscopy revealed long, crooked, branching, beaded gram-positive filaments
questions.lead_in: What would be the most appropriate empiric therapy?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and imipenem The patient is immunocompromised due to his transplantation and presents with a cavitary lung lesion. He is at risk for many opportunistic pathogens but has Gram stain findings suggestive of infection due to Nocardia. Two-drug therapy with sulfamethoxazole and imipenem would be recommended empirically and the patient will likely require a minimum of 6 months of treatment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q8

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presented with a 6-week history of a left buttock mass. It was nontender, and he was otherwise asymptomatic. He thought it may be related to a minor trauma when he scraped himself on a yucca plant while gardening. He had received an allogeneic stem cell transplant 9 months earlier for acute myelogenous leukemia, which had been complicated by graft versus host disease of the skin and gastrointestinal tract. He was taking prednisone 20 mg od, tacrolimus, inhaled pentamidine, and aciclovir. On examination, his temperature was 37°C, his blood pressure was 145/73 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturations 99% on room air. He was overweight, in no acute distress, and he had a grapefruit-sized mass on his left buttock. The rest of the exam was unremarkable. Investigations: Total white cell count 8.6 ×109/L Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL Platelets 146 ×109 /L eGFR >60 mL/min per 1.73 m2 Aspiration of the mass revealed gram-positive branching filamentous rods.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nocardia farcinica Nocardia farcinica is an opportunistic pathogen found in soil and water, which can cause skin and soft tissue infections when it gets into open wounds or cuts. The typical appearance on Gram stain is as gram-positive branching filamentous rods. Treatment of choice is trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole. Mycobacterium abscessus is a nontuberculous mycobacterium which would appear as acid-fast bacilli on acid-fast staining. It can cause nodular and ulcerative lesions in areas of trauma. Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is a multidrug-resistant gram-negative pathogen that can cause ventilator-associated pneumonia. Scedosporium prolificans is an opportunistic fungus that can cause infections in immunocompromised patients and would not appear as a gram-positive filamentous rod. Listeria monocytogenes would appear as a gram-positive rod on Gram stain, not filamentous, and causes meningitis in immunocompromised patients.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q26

questions.model_answer: a) Nocardia species. Beaded, branching Gram-positive filaments that are partially/modified acid-fast (Kinyoun positive), grow on standard aerobic media as dry, wrinkly (cerebriform/chalky) colonies over days, and grow on BCYE are characteristic of Nocardia, not a rapidly growing mycobacterium. b) Empirically, Nocardia is generally susceptible to TMP-SMX, linezolid, and amikacin; imipenem and ceftriaxone are variably active (species-dependent). Definitive treatment must be guided by species identification and broth microdilution susceptibility testing, as resistance varies by species (e.g., N. farcinica resistant to ceftriaxone; N. transvalensis complex resistant to amikacin/imipenem).
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort raised M. abscessus, but branching beaded filaments that are only partially/modified acid-fast plus growth on BCYE point to Nocardia rather than a rapidly growing mycobacterium.

questions.question_raw: Q8 (2006 PM). 35 year old male with Hodgkin's disease with lung nodules and ring-enhancing lesions in the brain.

parts.text: What is the most likely bacterial cause?

How would you treat this patient if he is allergic to penicillin?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the most likely bacterial cause?
b) How would you investigate (not including blood cultures)?
c) How would you treat this patient if he is allergic to penicillin?

questions.model_answer: a) Nocardia species (pulmonary nocardiosis with contiguous/haematogenous CNS spread); members of the former N. asteroides complex account for most systemic and CNS disease. b) (1) Repeated sputum and bronchoalveolar lavage for Gram stain (beaded, right-angled branching gram-positive filaments) plus modified acid-fast (modified Kinyoun) stain, aerobic bacterial, fungal and mycobacterial culture with prolonged incubation, alerting the laboratory that nocardiosis is suspected. (2) CT-guided aspiration/biopsy of a lung nodule for the same stains, culture and histopathology. (3) MRI brain (preferred imaging) to define the ring-enhancing lesions, with stereotactic aspiration/biopsy of a brain lesion for stain, culture and histology (early tissue diagnosis is warranted in the immunocompromised host given serious coexisting pathology). (4) Speciation and susceptibility testing by MALDI-TOF MS and/or 16S rRNA molecular identification, referring the isolate to a reference laboratory. c) This is disseminated disease with CNS involvement, so combination therapy is required; the mainstay is TMP-SMX (a sulfonamide, unaffected by penicillin allergy). Give a three-drug regimen of TMP-SMX plus a carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem) plus amikacin, empirically pending susceptibilities; linezolid is an effective alternative, particularly where renal impairment limits amikacin. Carbapenems are beta-lactams with low cross-reactivity to penicillin but can be replaced by amikacin/linezolid/ceftriaxone if a severe penicillin allergy precludes them. Treat parenterally for several weeks then step down to oral therapy, with a total duration of at least 12 months for CNS disease. Modify once speciation and susceptibilities return.

cohort_answer.text: a) Nocardia. DDx for lung/brain axis: bacterial (Rhodococcus equi, Anaerobes, S. anginosus, S. aureus, K. pneumoniae hypermucoviscous, Mycobacteria, Actinomyces), fungal (Aspergillus, Mucormycosis, Crypto neoformans). b) BAL; MRI brain (preferred in all suspected pulmonary/disseminated nocardiosis); lung nodule biopsy for cultures/pathology (nocardia culture, fungal culture, AFB, C/S); brain biopsy/aspirate for cultures/pathology; serum CrAg; BAL galactomannan. c) TMP-SMX + Imipenem + Amikacin first line for severe CNS disease (TMP-SMX monotherapy for CNS disease associated with >50% mortality); alternatives: linezolid, 3rd gen ceph (ceftriaxone/cefotaxime/cefuroxime) based on susceptibilities. IV therapy minimum 6 weeks then oral (minocycline, amoxicillin/clavulanate, fluoroquinolones, macrolides based on susceptibility). Total duration for CNS infection minimum 12 months.

questions.model_answer:
a) Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome.
b) Neutrophil oxidative burst test - dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry or nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT).
c) Defective NADPH oxidase in phagocytes: neutrophils cannot generate the oxidative (respiratory) burst, so they fail to kill catalase-positive bacteria and fungi.
d) Nocardia (branching, weakly/partially acid-fast on modified Kinyoun stain).
e) High-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; for severe/disseminated disease combine with a carbapenem (e.g., imipenem) +/- amikacin, with prolonged therapy.
f) Antifungal prophylaxis with itraconazole, and interferon-gamma.

parts.text: List three possible organisms and the first-line empiric treatment regimen for an immunosuppressed patient with ring-enhancing brain lesions and lung nodules.

parts_raw.text: Guy with vasculitis on steroids who has ring enhancing lesions in brain and lung nodules. List 3 possible organisms and first line empiric treatment regimen

questions.model_answer: Three organisms: (1) Nocardia species; (2) Staphylococcus aureus; (3) Streptococcus anginosus group (also consider Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus). Empiric regimen: cover pyogenic brain abscess (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin + metronidazole) PLUS anti-Nocardia therapy given the immunosuppression and combined brain/lung picture — TMP-SMX plus imipenem or meropenem, plus amikacin (or ceftriaxone/linezolid), then de-escalate after speciation and susceptibilities.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Nocardia arm is grounded in this chapter; the broader brain-abscess differential and empiric bacterial/TB/fungal coverage rest on standard CNS-infection references (Mandell brain abscess chapter/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Possible organisms: Nocardia, Staph aureus, Streptococcus anginosus. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone, vanco, metro (empiric bacterial coverage); Septra, imipenem +/- amikacin (Nocardia); TB - RIPE + steroids if meningitis; Cryptococcus - amphoB + flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.question: A patient has sporotrichoid spread; four different stains are shown and you must identify the organism for each.
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: picture of sporotrichoid spread with 4 different stains shown, asked to identify the organism for each]

parts.text: Stain 1 (Leishmania)
Stain of nocardia branching GPCs in chains
A gram stain with 30% GPC, rest looked either washed out or like GNC either solo or in short chains, clusters as well (Francisella tularensis)
Sporothrix stain, ~2microns in size (given legend up to 20 microns, nothing over 2-3 microns in size)

parts_raw.text: Stain 1 (Leischmania)
Stain of nocardia branching GPCs in chains
A gram stain with 30% GPC, rest looked either washed out or like GNC either solo or in short chains, clusters as well (Francisella tularensis)
Sporothrix stain, ~2microns in size (given legend up to 20 microns, nothing over 2-3 microns in size)

questions.model_answer: a) Leishmania spp. (intracellular amastigotes with nucleus and kinetoplast). b) Nocardia spp. (branching, beaded gram-positive filaments). c) Francisella tularensis (tiny, faintly-staining gram-negative coccobacilli; poorly-staining 'washed-out' gram appearance). d) Sporothrix schenckii (small ~1-3 microns cigar-shaped budding yeast).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the small cigar-shaped Sporothrix yeast (~1-3 x 3-10 microns) is grounded in the slice (p. 3134); the other identifications are standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text: Stain 1: Leishmania. Stain 2: Nocardia (branching GPCs in chains). Stain 3: Francisella tularensis (gram stain with ~30% GPC, rest washed out/GNC solo or in short chains/clusters). Stain 4: Sporothrix (~2 microns in size).

questions.question: Name four partially acid-fast organisms, then identify the organism shown growing as mucoid/salmon-colored colonies on an agar plate.
questions.question_raw: Q93 2023 Day 2. Name 4 partially acid-fast organisms. Then shown agar plate with mucoid/salmon colored colonies growing and asked to identify. (MICRO)

parts.text: Name four partially acid-fast organisms.
[image-based: identify the organism forming mucoid/salmon colored colonies on the agar plate shown]

parts_raw.text: Name 4 partially acid-fast organisms
[image-based: identify the organism forming mucoid/salmon colored colonies on the agar plate shown]

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Nocardia; (2) Rhodococcus; (3) Gordonia; (4) Tsukamurella — all aerobic, branching, partially acid-fast actinomycetes. b) Rhodococcus (Rhodococcus equi) — non-hemolytic, mucoid colonies with characteristic salmon-pink/orange pigment.
questions.beyond_mandell: The mucoid/salmon colony appearance of Rhodococcus is not described in this Nocardia chapter (standard microbiology reference).

cohort_answer.text:
4 partially acid-fast organisms: Nocardia spp; Rhodococcus; Gordonia; Tsukamurella (all partially acid-fast, aerobic, Actinomycetes, branching filamentous bacteria that fragment into rods and cocci).
Mucoid/salmon colonies: Rhodococcus spp - non-hemolytic, round, often mucoid with orange to red/salmon-pink pigment within 4-7 days. (For comparison: Nocardia colonies highly variable, some beta-hemolytic, wrinkly, dry, chalky-white to orange-tan, crumbly; Gordonia colonies smooth, mucoid, adherent, beige/orange/yellow/pink/white to gray; Tsukamurella colonies rhizoid edges, white or creamy to orange.)

questions.question: An immunocompromised patient (e.g., AML, or SLE on cyclophosphamide and prednisone) presents with dyspnea/respiratory symptoms and right-sided weakness. Imaging shows cavitary lung lesions and a brain lesion (brain abscess).
questions.question_raw:
Q17 (2011 PM) Brain + Lung lesions
AML patient presenting with dyspnea and R sided weakness. Cavitary lung lesions and one brain lesion
Alternate wording: SLE patient on cyclophosphamide and prednisone. Develops lung nodules and brain abscess. List 3 organisms and their tx?
List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

parts.text: List 3 organisms and the initial empiric treatment.

parts_raw.text: List 3 organisms and initial empiric tx?

questions.model_answer: a) Immunocompromised host (hematologic malignancy / cellular immune defect) with concurrent cavitary lung lesions and brain abscess points to pathogens that disseminate hematogenously from the lung to the CNS. Three organisms with empiric therapy: (1) Nocardia spp. — high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus a carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem), often with amikacin for serious/CNS disease; (2) Aspergillus spp. — voriconazole; (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis — four-drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) with corticosteroids. In practice, while awaiting aspiration/culture, many experts treat an immunocompromised patient empirically with high-dose meropenem (covers Nocardia, anaerobes, gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas, and possibly Listeria) plus voriconazole plus vancomycin (until MRSA excluded). (Other acceptable organisms: Cryptococcus neoformans — liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine; or Candida spp. in neutropenia.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific Nocardia regimen (TMP-SMX + carbapenem ± amikacin) and standard RIPE + steroids for TB follow IDSA/standard guidance; the chapter names the organisms and the meropenem + voriconazole + vancomycin empiric combination.

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia: TMP/SMX + imipenem/meropenem + amikacin. Aspergillus: Voriconazole. Tuberculosis: INH/RIF/ETH/PYZ + steroids. Cryptococcus neoformans: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (treatment phase) → Fluconazole (consolidation and suppressive phases). Actinomyces (A. meyeri, odontolyticus, israelii): Penicillin + surgery for CNS. Streptococcus anginosus: Ceftriaxone. S. aureus: Vancomycin.

questions.question: An immunocompromised patient (2010) develops pulmonary symptoms and is found to have lung nodules. Started empirically on piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin, the patient remains febrile and the lung nodules worsen. A sample is taken and Gram stain shows filamentous Gram-positive bacilli.
questions.question_raw: Q7 (2010 PM). Scenario with immunocompromised patient who develops pulmonary symptoms, found to have lung nodules. Started empirically on PipTazo and Vanco, continues to be febrile and lung nodules are worsening. Sample taken, and gram stain shows filamentous GPB.

parts.text: Most likely diagnosis
Single most important test at this point
Two other aerobic Gram-positive rods that can cause a similar picture

parts_raw.text: A) Most likely diagnosis
B) Single most important test at this point
C) Two other aerobic gram positive rods that can cause a similar picture

questions.model_answer: a) Pulmonary nocardiosis (Nocardia species). b) Modified acid-fast stain (e.g., modified Kinyoun) — Nocardia is partially acid-fast, distinguishing it from Actinomyces (not acid-fast). c) (1) Rhodococcus (R. equi); (2) Gordonia (also Tsukamurella/Streptomyces).

cohort_answer.text: A) Pulmonary nocardiosis. B) AFB stain - modified acid-fast staining (Kinyoun stain or auramine-rhodamine fluorescent stain) can make presumptive diagnosis; Nocardia differentiated from Actinomyces by acid-fastness and aerobic growth. C) Rhodococcus equi, Gordonia.
